**Sūrat al-Mumtaḥanah (The Chapter of the Woman Tested)**

Ibn Ḥajar said: The well-known pronunciation of this name is with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ (*al-Mumtaḥanah*), though it may also be read with a kasrah. On the first reading, the name describes the woman because of whom the chapter was revealed. On the second, it describes the chapter itself, as Barāʾah was called *al-Fāḍiḥah* (the Disgracer). In *Jamāl al-Qurrāʾ*, it is also called *Sūrat al-Imtiḥān* and *Sūrat al-Mawaddah*. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them, stated without qualification that it is Madinan (*Madaniyyah*). Some have mentioned that its first verses were revealed on the day of the conquest of Makkah. Its being Madinan is either by way of *taghlīb* (the predominant classification, where the majority determines the label) or based on the view that the Madinan is whatever was revealed after the Hijrah. It has thirteen verses, by consensus.

Its connection to what precedes it is that the previous chapter mentioned the alliance of those who feigned faith with those among the People of the Book who disbelieved. This chapter mentions the prohibition on the believers taking the disbelievers as allies, lest they resemble the hypocrites, and it explains this matter in full detail. It has also been said that the previous chapter mentioned the People of the Book who had covenants with the Muslims, while this chapter mentions those among the polytheists who had covenants, because it contains what was revealed concerning the Treaty of al-Ḥudaybiyyah. Because of the close connection between this chapter and the one before it, the chapter of *al-Ṣaff* was placed between them, though *al-Ṣaff* and this chapter both begin with *Sabbaḥa* (glorify).

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ was revealed concerning Ḥāṭib ibn ʿAmr Abī Balt͟aʿah, who was the client (*mawlā*) of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥumayd ibn Zuhayr ibn Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā. Imam Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Ḥibbān, and a group of others reported from ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent me, al-Zubayr, and al-Miqdād, and said: "Go until you reach Rawḍat Khākh, for there is a woman traveling with a letter. Take it from her and bring it to me." We set out until we reached the garden, and there we found the woman. We said: "Bring out the letter." She said: "I have no letter with me." We said: "You will either bring out the letter or we will strip off your clothes." So she took it out from her braid, and we brought it to the Prophet (ﷺ). In it was: "From Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Balt͟aʿah to some people among the polytheists in Makkah, informing them of some of the affairs of the Prophet (ﷺ)." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What is this, O Ḥāṭib?!" He said: "Do not rush to judgment against me, O Messenger of Allah. I was a man attached to Quraysh but I was not one of them by origin. Those of your companions who were with you, the Emigrants, have relatives who protect their families and property in Makkah. I wished, since I lacked a blood tie with them, to do them a favor so that they would protect my relatives. I did not do this out of disbelief or apostasy from my religion." ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Let me strike his neck, O Messenger of Allah." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He fought at Badr. What would make you know? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: 'Do as you wish, for I have forgiven you.'" Then this verse was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾.

In a narration of Ibn Mardawayh from Anas: The Prophet (ﷺ) sent ʿUmar and ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them both, after that woman. They overtook her on the road but could not get anything from her. They turned back, and then one of them said to the other: "By Allah, we have not been lied to, nor have we lied. Let us go back to her." They returned, drew their swords, and said: "By Allah, we will make you taste death, or you will hand over the letter." She denied it, then said: "I will hand it to you on the condition that you do not return me to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." They agreed, and she brought it out to them from the locks of her hair.

According to *al-Durr al-Manthūr*, the woman is called Umm Sārah and was a client of Quraysh. In *al-Kashshāf*, it is said that she is called Sārah, a client of Abū ʿAmr ibn Ṣayfī ibn Hāshim. The soundness of Anas's report is questionable, and what it contains of the return of the two Imams, may Allah be pleased with them both, is improbable. It has also been said that those sent after her were ʿUmar, ʿAlī, Ṭalḥah, al-Zubayr, ʿAmmār, al-Miqdād, and Abū Marthad, and that they were horsemen. But what is relied upon is what we have already mentioned. Those who were with Ḥāṭib in Makkah were his sons and brothers, as reported from ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥāṭib mentioned above. In a narration of Aḥmad from Jābir, Ḥāṭib said: "My mother was with them." It is possible that she was with his sons and brothers.

The form of the letter, according to some narrations, was: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has set out toward you with an army like the night, moving like a torrent. I swear by Allah that if he came toward you alone, Allah would give him victory over you, for He surely fulfills what He has promised him." It has been said that the previous report is evidence for the permissibility of killing a spy, since the Prophet (ﷺ) gave as a reason for withholding the punishment his attendance at Badr. (But this is open to discussion.) In describing the polytheists as "enemy," with the attribution to His pronoun, Mighty and Majestic is He, there is an emphasis on the gravity of taking them as allies, and an indication that the punishment of Allah the Exalted will befall them. There is also an allusion to the meaning of the line of poetry:

*When the friend of your enemy is friendly toward you, he has become hostile to you, and speech is cut off.*

The word *ʿaduww* (enemy) is of the pattern *fa'ūl*, like *ʿafuww* from *ʿafā*. Because it is of the form of a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), it is used for the plural as it is used for the singular. *Awliyāʾ* is in the accusative as the second object of *tattakhidhū* (take). The words ﴿you convey affection to them﴾ either explain *al-muwālāh* (alliance) or the act of taking them as allies, or they are a new sentence and have no place in the *iʿrāb* (grammatical analysis). The *bāʾ* is extra in the object, as in His saying: ﴿and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195]. Conveying affection here is a metaphor for displaying it. Explaining it as "delivering" does not remove the figurative sense. It has also been said that the *bāʾ* indicates transitivity, the meaning being "you convey affection to them," and *afḍā* is transitive with *bāʾ*, as in *al-Asās*. It has also been said that the *bāʾ* marks cause, and that the verb "convey" is metaphorical for "send": "you send them the news of the Prophet (ﷺ) because of the affection that is between you." The Basrans held that the preposition is linked to the verbal noun implied by the verb, and that in this case the verbal noun is omitted while its complement remains. It is also permitted that the clause be a circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl*) from the subject of *lā tattakhidhū*, or a descriptive phrase (*ṣifah*) modifying *awliyāʾ*. The Qur'an did not say "you convey affection to them" with the explicit pronoun, on the ground that such a pronoun is not obligatory with a descriptive phrase that refers to someone other than the one it describes, or with a circumstantial phrase, predicate, or relative clause, whether the element is a noun or a verb, as is stated in Ibn Mālik's *Sharḥ al-Tashīl*, provided that no ambiguity arises. For example, *Zayd Hind ḍāribuhā* or *yaḍribuhā* is fine, but *Zayd ʿAmr ḍāribuhu* or *yaḍribuhu* requires the explicit pronoun *huwa*, because of the ambiguity.

[p. 67]

Some have claimed that the explicit pronoun is required only with nouns in such descriptive phrases, not with verbs as here, but this has been rejected. Both explanations have been criticized on the ground that they give the impression that alliance is permitted when conveying affection does not occur. This would require the view that the prohibition on alliance does not have an implicit contrary meaning (*mafhūm*) in general, apart from this verse. Alternatively, it could be said that the circumstantial phrase and the descriptive phrase are necessary, and that is why the clause explains the matter. His saying: ﴿while they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth﴾ is a circumstantial phrase from the subject of *lā tattakhidhū*. It is a parallel circumstantial phrase if the clause ﴿you convey affection﴾ is itself circumstantial, or it is from the subject of *tulqūn*, in which case it is overlapping, given that the latter is circumstantial. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial phrase from the object, or a new sentence.

Al-Jaḥdarī and al-Muʿallā, from ʿĀṣim, read *limā* with a *lām*, meaning "because of what has come to you." This makes what is the cause of faith the cause of disbelief. ﴿They expel the Messenger and you﴾, that is, from Makkah, ﴿because you believe in Allah, your Lord﴾, that is, because of your faith or out of hatred for your belief in Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. The prepositional phrase is linked to *yukhrijūna*. The clause has been said to be either a circumstantial phrase from the subject of *kafarū*, or a new sentence that explains their disbelief, as if it were asked: "How did they disbelieve?" The answer is that they disbelieved in the worst way, by expelling the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers simply because of their faith, not for any other reason. This explanation is preferred over the first for its fit with the context and its many benefits. The present tense is used to bring the past situation vividly before the mind, because of its added enormity. The continuous sense does not fit the meaning. Regarding ﴿you believe﴾, it has been said that the expression is a form of *taghlīb* (predominance of the believers). There is also a shift (*iltifāt*) from the first-person pronoun, that is, from "Me" to the expression of the sublime text, which would be "by Me." This is to indicate what makes faith obligatory: divinity and lordship.

﴿If you have gone out to strive in My way and seeking My pleasure﴾ is connected to His saying: ﴿do not take﴾, and so on, as if it were said: "Do not befriend My enemies if you are My allies." The conditional clause's response is omitted and is understood from what precedes. Al-Zamakhsharī made it a circumstantial phrase from the subject of *lā tattakhidhū* and did not assign it a response, meaning: "Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, while you have gone out for the sake of striving and seeking My pleasure." This was objected to on the ground that a conditional clause does not occur as a circumstantial phrase without a response, except in the concessive *in* (even if), which requires the *wāw* and is used where the opposite of what is mentioned is more likely, as in "Be kind to Zayd, even if he mistreats you." The present case is not like that.

It was answered that Ibn Jinnī permitted it, and Jār Allah (al-Zamakhsharī) approved it here, because eloquence and the flow of speech require it. One says to someone whose friendship is established, without any intent of conditionality or doubt: "Do not abandon me if you are my friend," to arouse zeal. There is in this usage what there is of beauty, so it does no harm that it departs from what is well-known. The two verbal nouns are in the accusative as causal objects, as we indicated. It is also permitted that they be circumstantial: "striving and seeking." The "going out" may mean either going out to fight or emigrating. The address is to the Emigrants specifically, since the incident came from them, as you have heard in the account of the occasion of revelation.

His saying: ﴿you confide to them with affection﴾ is an explanatory resumption, as if they, sensing the rebuke for what preceded, asked: "What did we do that caused us to be rebuked?" It was said: "You confide ..." It is also permitted that it be a substitute for *tulqūn* (you convey), a substitution of a whole for a whole if *ilqāʾ* is meant as secret conveying, or a substitution of a part if the more general meaning is intended, since secret and open are both included in it. Abū Ḥayyān said: It resembles *badal al-ishtimāl* (substitution of inclusion). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "You are the ones who confide," and the sentence is a resumption for rebuke against them. You know that the resumption for this purpose is good, but it does not require an omission. The meaning of the *bāʾ* here is as their statements suggest, like the *bāʾ* previously.

His saying: ﴿And I am most knowing of what you conceal and what you declare﴾

[p. 68]

is in the position of a circumstantial phrase. "*Aʿlamu*" (I am most knowing) is a comparative form (*ism tafḍīl*), and the element compared to is omitted, meaning "than you." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah permitted that it be a present-tense verb. Knowledge may take *bāʾ* as its complement, or the *bāʾ* is extra. *Mā* is either a relative pronoun or a verbal source. He mentioned "what you declare" although it could be omitted, to indicate that the two kinds of knowledge are equal in His knowledge, Mighty and Majestic is He. For this reason, "what you conceal" was placed first. This circumstantial phrase also indicates that there is no benefit for them in confiding affection to them. It is as if it were said: "You confide to them with affection, while I know what you conceal and what you declare, and I inform My Messenger of what you confide. So what benefit or use is there for you in secrecy?"

﴿And whoever of you does that﴾, that is, the confiding, ﴿has indeed strayed from the right way﴾. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and a group said: that is, taking them as allies, ﴿from among you﴾. ﴿Has strayed from the right way﴾ means the straight path and the true road. The construction *sawāʾ* (of the way) is of the type of the descriptive phrase joined to the described noun. It is in the accusative as the object of *ḍalla* (he strayed), which is transitive like *aḍalla* (he led astray). It has been said that *ḍalla* is not transitive, and that *sawāʾ* is an adverbial of place, like the line of poetry:

*as ʿasala al-ṭarīq* ("as the [wolf] hurried along the road")

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 60, verse 2:

﴿If they overcome you﴾, meaning if they gain the upper hand over you. The root of *thaqf* is skill in grasping a thing and doing it, and from it comes the phrase *rajul thaqif laqif* (a man who is quick and adept). It is used figuratively for gaining the upper hand and for attaining something in general. ﴿They will be enemies to you﴾, meaning enmity that results in actual harm, as evidenced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they will stretch out their hands and their tongues against you with evil﴾, meaning with what harms you, such as killing, capture, and reviling. So this is an explanatory conjunction (*'atf tafsiri*). The clause ﴿they will be﴾ and so on is the response of the condition according to the consideration we have pointed to. Otherwise, their being enemies to the addressees is something established before the condition, as evidenced by what is at the beginning of the surah. A similar view is that of some scholars: that is, they will manifest what is in their hearts of enmity and will apply its rulings to it. It has also been said that what is meant is the necessary consequence of enmity and its fruit, which is the manifestation of the uselessness of showing affection, so it is as if it were said: if they overcome you, there will become evident to you the uselessness of offering them affection and showing love to them. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they wish that you would disbelieve﴾ is conjoined to the response, and it is in the future in meaning, as is the nature of the response. It may be interpreted, as its predecessor was interpreted, by saying, according to what is in *al-Kashf*, that what is meant is a love that results in the capacity to return you to disbelief. Or it may be said, according to what some have said, that what is meant is the display of love and the carrying out of what it requires. The expression in the past tense, although the meaning is future, serves to indicate that their love is their disbelief before everything else, and that it is present even if they do not overcome you.

The explanation of this is that love is prior in kind but later with respect to some individual instances. So it is expressed in the past tense with regard to the first, and it is made a delayed response with regard to the second. Al-Khatib al-Dimashqi preferred the conjunction to be with the whole conditional sentence, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they will not be helped﴾ [al-Hashr: 12] in the surah before ﴿So when their term comes, they will not delay an hour nor advance it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34], according to a group who said: because their love that they should revert to disbelief is present even if they do not overcome you, so there is no benefit in the restriction by the condition. Abu Hayyan went to this view. Its answer is known from what we have mentioned. Close to this is what has been said: since the love of their disbelief after gaining the upper hand was not apparent, because at that time they are captives and servants who are not counted, it is permissible that their disbelief is not desired, so it requires informing about it. In contrast, the love before gaining the upper hand is a different and later love, so the restriction has a benefit. Some of the eminent scholars said: the conjoined element after the conditional in the speech of the Arabs comes in several ways. The first is that each of the two is both a response and a cause, as in: if you come to me, I will come to you and give you. The second is that the response is one of them, and the other is mentioned because of its strong connection to it, being its cause, for example: when the commander came, I asked permission and went out to receive him; and: I detained my debtor so that I might collect my right and release him.

The third is that the intended meaning is the combination of two matters, and in that case the earlier occurrence of one of them does not contradict it, for example: I went out with the pilgrims so that I might accompany them on the going, and I did not accompany them on the return. From this is His saying, exalted is He:
