﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear victory﴾ ﴿That Allah may forgive you your earlier and later sins﴾ [al-Fath: 1, 2], and so on. What is in this sublime composition here has been said to be susceptible to the first, because the love is future from some considerations, as has preceded, and it is expressed in the past tense in consideration of the rank of precedence, in that returning them to disbelief is the most grievous of harms according to the disbelievers, since they know that religion is dearer to the believers than their souls, for they expend their souls in its defense. And the most important thing to the enemy is to aim at the most important thing to his opponent. It is also susceptible to the third, by taking what is meant as the combination, with the interpretation: they desire for you the harms of this world and the next. It has been said that it is also susceptible to the second, with the response being ﴿they stretch out﴾, and their enmity and their love are mentioned in the form of return because of the strength of the connection between them, since there is causation and being caused. This is, as you see, far-fetched. Al-Tibi regarded the combination as a metaphor through the use of the cause to mean the effect, namely the harms of the two abodes. He mentioned that the response is in reality omitted, meaning: they desire for you the harms of the world and religion, and what has been mentioned is its evidence, which has been put in its place. It has been said: the past tense was used for love in order to indicate that its realization among the believers is more complete than the realization of what precedes it, and a statement of the author of *al-Miftah* has been interpreted accordingly.

It is reported from some of them that the *waw* is the *waw* of circumstance, not the *waw* of conjunction, and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase, with *qad* implied or not implied. It is not hidden that conjunction is the more immediate sense, and that its being conjoined to the response is more remote in purpose. The instances of conditional and response constructions of this kind are more than can be counted.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 60, verse 3:

﴿Your relatives and your children will never benefit you﴾ This is a rebuttal of what might be imagined as a valid excuse, namely that the motive for taking them as allies and showing affection to them is the preservation of relatives and children from harm by those (the disbelievers). The rahim (womb, kinship) in its original sense is the womb of a woman, but it became well known for kinship (qarabah) until it became, as it were, a literal term for it. So either it is meant in that sense, or it is taken as a metaphor for a close relative, or a noun is understood with it, i.e. dhawu arhamikum (those of your wombs/kin). The interpretation is supported by the conjunction of the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿nor your children﴾, meaning: your kinsfolk or your relatives will never benefit you, nor will your children, those for whose sake you befriend the polytheists and draw near to them, defending them, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, by warding off harm or bringing benefit. ﴿He will separate between you﴾ is a resumed statement explaining that relatives and children will benefit no one on that day; that is, Allah the Exalted will separate you from one another by the terror that will occur, which causes each of you to flee from the other, as expressed by the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿On the Day a man will flee from his brother﴾ [Abasa: 34] and so on. Therefore the right of Allah the Exalted should not be abandoned, and His enemies should not be befriended, by one whose situation is this. What we have indicated, that the Day of Resurrection is connected to the verb preceding it, is the apparent reading, but it has also been permitted that it be connected to the verb "yafsilu" that follows it.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Wathhab read "yufassilu" with a damma on the ya' and a shaddah on the sad, in the active voice. Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi Ablah read likewise, except that they lightened it. Talhah and al-Nakha'i read "nufassilu" with the nun vowelled with a damma, the shaddah, and the active voice. These two, as well as Zayd ibn Ali, read it with a fathah on the nun, lightened, in the active voice. Abu Haywah also read it with a damma on the nun.

Al-A'raj, Isa and Ibn Amir read "yufassalu" with the ya', the shaddah, and the passive voice. The majority of readers are likewise, except that they lightened it. The deputy of the verb (na'ib al-fa'il) is either ﴿baynakum﴾ (between you), which is built on the fathah because it is attached to something that is deeply indeclinable (mutawaghghil fi al-bina'), as has been said; or it is the pronoun of the verbal noun understood from the verb, i.e. "yafsilu huwa", that is, the separation itself. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, so He will recompense you for it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 60, verse 4 (part 1 of 2):

﴿There has indeed been for you an excellent example in Ibrahim and those with him﴾. This emphasizes the matter of rebuke against them and the error of allying with the disbelievers, through the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and those with him, so that it may be known that loving for the sake of God Most High and hating for His sake, glorified be He, are among the most secure handholds of faith, and so neither of them should be neglected. The word *uswah* (example, pattern) may be pronounced with a *damma* or a *kasra* on the *hamza*, and both are dialectal variants. Al-Kasa'i (no, rather: all the readers except ʿĀṣim) recited it with a *kasra*. It means *i'tisa'* (taking as a model) and *iqtida'* (following). It may also be applied to the quality that ought to be taken as a model and followed, and to the person himself who is taken as a model.

[p. 70]

Thus one may say "in Zayd there is an example" by way of *tajrid* (a rhetorical device in which a figure is abstracted from a subject, here meaning a person is referred to as the embodiment of a quality), as in the verse: "For the weak there is a sufficient one in the Most Merciful / and in the helmet there are twenty *mann* of iron." Each of these has been said to be possible in the verse. The meaning of the quality is preferred, because the exception that follows is more apparent in light of it. The *lakum* (for you) is for explanation (*bayan*) and is connected to an omitted element, as in *suqya laka* (water for you). Alternatively, it is connected to *kana* (was), according to the view of those who permit a adverbial phrase to be connected to it. *Uswatun* is its subject and *hasanatun* is its adjective, and *fi Ibrahim* is its predicate. Or *lakum* is the predicate, and *fi Ibrahim* is an adjective after an adjective (modifying *uswah*), or a predicate after a predicate (for *kana*), or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *lakum* according to what has been said, or from the pronoun in *hasanah*. It was not permitted that it be a complement of *uswah*, on the basis that *uswah* is a verbal noun, or its subject, and a qualified (described) subject does not govern in any absolute sense because of the weakness of its resemblance to the verb. It has been said: if we say that it is neither a verbal noun nor its subject, or we say that its governing is excused even if it is described before it governs the adverbial phrase, because of the latitude in such phrases, then that is permitted.

The apparent meaning is that by "those with him" (peace be upon him) is meant his believing followers. However, al-Tabari and a group said: what is meant by them are the prophets who lived near his time (peace be upon them all), because he (peace be upon him) did not have believing followers with him at the time of his confrontation with his people and his disavowal of them, who would confront them with him and disavow them. It is related that when he migrated to Syria from the land of Namrud, he said to Sarah: "On earth there is no one who worships God Most High besides me and you." And you know that the existence of believing followers at the very start of the confrontation is not necessarily required; rather what is required is their existence at some point later. And there is no doubt that they did exist later, so "those with him" should be understood as referring to them. The disavowal mentioned in the words of God Most High, ﴿when they said to their people: "Indeed we are free of you"﴾ and so on, refers to the time of their existence. *Idh* (when) has been said to be an adverbial element related to the predicate of *kanat* (was), and the governing element is the prepositional phrase or the complement, or it is *kana* itself as already explained, or it is a substitute for *uswah*. *Bura'* (free of) is the plural of *bari'*, like *zarif* and *zurafa'*.

Al-Jahdari recited *bira'* like *zirafin*, the plural of *zarif* as well. Abu Ja'far recited *bura'* with a *damma* on the *ba'*, like *tu'am* and *zu'ar*, which is a collective noun whose singular is *bari'*, *tuwam* and *zi'r*. Al-Zamakhshari said that this is by the substitution of a *damma* for a *kasra*, like *rukhal* with a *damma* on the *ra'*, the plural of *rakhil*. This was objected to on the grounds that this *damma* is original, and the form is among the patterns of collective nouns, not a broken plural, so the *damma* would not be a replacement for the *kasra*. This reading is narrated from ʿĪsā, and Abu Hatim said: "They claim it is ʿĪsā al-Hamdani, and from him is *bara'* on the pattern *fa'al*, like what is in the words of God Most High, ﴿Indeed I am free of what you worship﴾ in Surah al-Zukhruf: 26. It is a verbal noun on the pattern *fa'al*, which is applied to a singular or otherwise." The emphasis of the sentence is for greater attention to its matter, or because their people, the polytheists, were disbelieving in that and doubting it, since they imagined themselves to be upon something. And it is as if they sensed that from them, so they said to them: ﴿Indeed we are free of you﴾.

﴿And of what you worship besides God﴾, of idols and stars and others, ﴿we have rejected you﴾. This is an explanation of His words, glorified be He, ﴿Indeed we are free﴾ and what follows. So it means "we have rejected you and what you worship besides God." What is meant by "you" is the people and their objects of worship, by way of the predominance of the addressees. The rejection in this sense is a metaphor or an allusion to not regarding them as of any account, as if it were said: "We do not reckon your affair nor the affair of your gods, and you are not of any importance to us."

In *al-Kashf* it is stated that the original form was "we have rejected what you worship," and then "we have rejected you and what you worship," because whoever rejects what a person brings has rejected him. Then he suffices with "our rejection of you," since it includes rejection of all that they brought and all that they were involved in, especially since "Indeed we are free" preceded it and was explained as "we do not reckon" and so on, indicating that it is a mockery of them, for that is not called disbelief linguistically or customarily. It is rather a name applied to the most blameworthy and reprehensible things. What we have mentioned is closer, and it is the meaning of what is in *al-Kashshaf* but without it. As for what has been said, that there is in the sentence an omitted element coordinated with the prepositional phrase, namely "with you and with what you worship," and it was omitted as sufficient by the indication of context, this is not valid.

[p. 71]

﴿And enmity and hatred have appeared between us and you, forever﴾. That is, this is our practice with you, which we do not abandon, ﴿until you believe in God alone﴾, and abandon what you are upon of polytheism. Then the enmity will turn into friendship and the hatred into love. Al-Fayruzabadi explained *al-baghda'* (hatred) as intense hatred, the opposite of love, and stated that enmity is the opposite of friendship, and he explained friendship as love. So enmity and hatred, on this basis, are close in meaning. Al-Raghib stated that enmity is the opposition of harmony in the heart, and said: *al-bughd* is the recoil of the soul from a thing that one dislikes, and it is the opposite of love. Then he said: it is said "he hated the thing with hatred, a hatred, and hatred (*baghda'*)", and this is similar to the words of al-Fayruzabadi. What appears from the words of more than one scholar is that in enmity one often considers abandonment or withdrawal of support, rather than hatred. So let this matter be examined.

﴿Except the saying of Ibrahim to his father: "I will surely ask forgiveness for you"﴾. This is an exception from the words of God Most High, ﴿an excellent example﴾, as stated by Qatadah and a group. It is on the basis of the abstraction, or of interpreting *uswah* as following, and it is certainly *munqati'* (disconnected exception, where the excluded item is not of the same category as the preceding). As for when *uswah* is taken to mean the thing that is taken as a model, it has been said to be *muttasil* (connected exception, where the excluded item is of the same category), and it has been said to be *munqati'*, and this is what most scholars hold. The exception is directed to the promise of seeking forgiveness, not to the act of seeking forgiveness itself which is related from him (peace be upon him) in the words of God Most High, ﴿and forgive my father﴾ in Surah al-Shu'ara': 86 and so on, even though the latter is what is meant. It has been said: this is because the promise was what moved him (peace be upon him) to it. From this it is known that the act of seeking forgiveness itself is excluded by way of greater inference. Some have taken it as an allusion to seeking forgiveness, because the promise of a noble person, especially one like Ibrahim (peace be upon him), is especially when confirmed with an oath, usually followed by fulfillment, but this is not a necessary entailment, as is not hidden. And it seems this promise is other than the earlier promise in Surah Maryam: 47, in the words of God Most High, quoted from him (peace be upon him): ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾ and so on. Perhaps it was made by him (peace be upon him) after that as an affirmation of it, and it is related here by way of exception.

In *al-Irshad* it is stated that its specification in mention, rather than what occurred in Surah Maryam, is because it occurred in the form of an emphatic oath. The exclusion of that from the excellent example has been said to be because his (peace be upon him) seeking forgiveness for his disbelieving father, in the sense that God Most High would grant him repentance and guide him to faith, although it was permissible rationally and legally, since it occurred before it became clear that he was among the people of the blazing fire and that he would die upon disbelief, as indicated by what is in Surah al-Tawbah, nevertheless it is not something that ought to be taken as a model at all. For what is meant by a model is that which must necessarily be followed, since a threat is attached to turning away from it in the words of God Most High after this: ﴿And whoever turns away, then indeed God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy﴾. So his exclusion from what preceded only indicates that it is not obligatory to request faith and forgiveness for a disbeliever whose faith is hoped for, and no sensible person doubts this. As for its impermissibility, the exception provides no definitive indication of it. And Imam ʿAlī claimed what has been related from him, that the verse indicates that. It does not follow that seeking forgiveness on his part (peace be upon him) was a sin, because many of the special characteristics of the prophets (peace be upon them) are not permissible to emulate, since they were permitted to them alone. This is, as you see, [unsatisfactory], for it is clear that the seeking of forgiveness which occurred from him (peace be upon him), if it were supposed to have occurred from another, would have been a sin, and it is not so. Rather it is permissible for the one from whom it occurred.

From al-Tibi there is something whose gist is this: when Ibrahim (peace be upon him) answered his father's words, ﴿Indeed I will stone you, so leave me for a long time﴾ (Maryam: 46), with the words ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾ out of compassion and tenderness toward him, and he did not know of his persistence in disbelief, he fulfilled his promise and said ﴿and forgive my father﴾. Then when his persistence became clear, he abandoned the supplication and disavowed him. It thus becomes evident that his seeking forgiveness was not condemned, and that was during his father's lifetime, unlike what we are concerned with, for [the verse] has detailed their enmity and their eagerness to sever their kinship ties with the words of God Most High, ﴿will not benefit you﴾ and so on, and consoled them concerning severance with the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Then it excepted from this what was mentioned, as if it were said: do not be lenient with them and do not show them compassion as Ibrahim did, because it had not become clear to him as it has become clear to you. End of quotation. And in this there is an allusion to the possibility that the excepted item is the promise itself insofar as it indicates compassion and mercy, and the result of that is the exception of compassion and mercy.

Some eminent scholars gave as the reason why his (peace be upon him) seeking forgiveness for his disbelieving father is not something to be taken as a model, that it occurred before the prohibition, or because of a promise he had made to him. The second was objected to on the ground that a promise to do what is forbidden does not lift its prohibition. The first was objected to on the ground that it is based on the prohibition applying to his (peace be upon him) seeking forgiveness for him, even though the prohibition was revealed only concerning seeking forgiveness after the matter had become clear, and his (peace be upon him) seeking forgiveness had occurred before that. It also indicates that seeking forgiveness would have been a model if it had not been prohibited, although what is to be taken as a model is what must necessarily be followed, not what is permissible to do in general. It was answered with something that does not remove the dispute. So the better explanation is the one already mentioned.

Abu Hayyan maintained that the exception is from an omitted genitive attached to Ibrahim, that is, in the composition of the noble verse, "There has indeed been for you an excellent example in the sayings of Ibrahim and his disputes with his people, ﴿except the saying of Ibrahim﴾" and so on. He held definitively that the exception is connected on this reading. Likewise al-Tibi held definitively that it is connected according to the view of al-Baghawi, meaning: "for you there is an excellent example in Ibrahim and his affairs, except in his seeking forgiveness for his polytheist father." It is not hidden that this supposition is contrary to the apparent meaning, and if it is adopted, it is better to suppose "affairs" as the omitted element. It remains that it has been said that the verse indicates a prohibition against emulating Ibrahim (peace be upon him) in seeking forgiveness for a living disbeliever, even though in the sense mentioned earlier, namely asking that he be granted faith, there is no prohibition against it.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 60, verse 4 (part 2 of 2):

It has been answered that he was only forbidden to follow its apparent meaning, and it was assumed that it was permissible absolutely, as occurred to some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. In this there is the point that it has already been established that the indication of the verse is that seeking forgiveness is not something that must be followed definitively, not that it is forbidden and unlawful. Then it should be known that the clarification that his father was among the people of the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim), before which the seeking of forgiveness had taken place, occurred in this world, and likewise the disavowal of him after it. It has already been mentioned in the commentary on Surah al-Tawbah that there is an opinion that this occurred in the Hereafter, based on the apparent meanings of some authentic reports, for they indicate that he (ﷺ) will intercede for his father on the Day of Resurrection, and that intercession is a form of seeking forgiveness, that is, a seeking of forgiveness within it. Had it been clarified that he would die a disbeliever in this world, he would not have interceded and sought, in the most complete manner, forgiveness for him, since it is necessary that he (ﷺ) knew that Allah, exalted is He, does not forgive that He be associated with. Denying this is something that no sensible person would hardly venture. As for those who hold that the clarification occurred in this world, as the predecessors of the Ummah held, and this is the correct view which I am certain of today, those apparent meanings became problematic for them in terms of their indication of intercession, which on that Day is a form of seeking forgiveness. They exerted themselves and succeeded in answering them. All that I have found for them has already been mentioned, so return to it and choose for yourself what pleases you.

Then I say: what prevails upon my assessment is that the seeking of forgiveness that came from him (ﷺ) before the clarification was in the well-known sense, not in the sense of granting success to faith. The verses in Surah al-Tawbah and what has been reported regarding the occasion of their revelation support its apparent meanings in this regard.

And I maintain that the prohibition of permissibility of seeking forgiveness was known only through revelation, not through reason, because it is possible that Allah, exalted is He, forgives the disbeliever, and He, glorified is He, is the Most Forgiving, the Most Merciful. And when he (ﷺ) sought forgiveness, he was not aware, through revelation, of its prohibition. The meaning of the verse, and Allah, exalted is He, knows best, is: for you there is the example of Abraham (ʿalayhi al-salam) and those with him in disavowal of the disbelievers. But his seeking forgiveness for the disbeliever is not an example for you to follow, and what is required of you is disavowal and it is forbidden for you to seek forgiveness or show compassion. So the exception that we have considered is not, for you, from the category of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113], and so on. The indication of that toward prohibition is evident, so reflect upon everything we have presented. Behind this there is a discussion based on the view of the one who said: Allah, exalted and majestic is He, has no binding decree. This was reported from al-Qutb al-Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qadir al-Kilani, may his secret be sanctified. Some eminent scholars erected its pillars in a separate treatise, in which they expounded the proofs for that, but it is not free from scrutiny, and Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Nor can I obtain for you anything from Allah﴾ is part of the stated speech, and its place in i'rab is accusative (naṣb), as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of ﴿I will surely seek forgiveness for you﴾. The object of the exception is the seeking of forgiveness itself, not its qualifier, for in itself it is among the good qualities, since it is a display of helplessness and a committing of the matter to Allah, exalted is He. So the statement is of the type in which negation returns to the qualified, not to the qualifier.

In al-Kashf: although it is in itself a statement that conforms to reality and it is good to make it an example, he attached to it His saying: ﴿I will surely seek forgiveness for you﴾ as a confirmation of the promise, as if it were said: "I will surely seek forgiveness for you, and what is within my power is only this, so it is certainly offered." And in this there is that had he possessed more than that, he would have done it. On this basis, it is deserving of the exception. His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have turned in repentance, and to You is the final return﴾, to the end of the verse, is a resumed sentence with no place in i'rab, connected in meaning to the story of Abraham (ʿalayhi al-salam) and those with him, in that it explains their state in striving against the enemies of Allah, exalted and majestic is He, and in the hardship of struggle, then their turning to Allah, exalted is He, for the sufficiency against their evil, and that this is from them directed to Him, glorified and majestic is He, not for the sake of their own portion. It has also been said that its connection with what preceded is verbal, on the basis that it is governed by an implied saying, coordinated with ﴿They said to their people: Indeed, we are free of you﴾, meaning: "and they said: Our Lord..." And it is permitted that the meaning is: "Say: Our Lord," as a command from Him, exalted is He, to the believers to say it, and as a teaching from Him, mighty and majestic is He, to them, and a completion of what He, glorified is He, had enjoined upon them of severing ties between them and the disbelievers, and following Abraham (ʿalayhi al-salam) and his people in disavowing them, and an alert to turning to Allah, exalted is He, and seeking refuge in Him from the trial of the people of disbelief, and seeking forgiveness for what had transpired from them. This, as it has been said, is a good aspect that the noble composition does not reject. In it there is a trace of the style of ﴿Desist; it is better for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 171], because when He, glorified is He, urged them to follow the example of those you have heard about in desisting from disbelief and allying with its people, then said, glorified is He, what indicates turning to Him, exalted is He, it becomes in meaning a prohibition of the first and a command of the second.

Some of them made the saying in this aspect coordinated with "Do not take," meaning: "and say: Our Lord..." Whichever it is, the fronting of the prepositional phrase in the three places is for restriction, as if it were said: "Our Lord, upon You alone we have relied, not upon other than You; and to You alone we have turned in repentance, not to other than You; and to You alone is the final return, not to other than You."

﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve﴾. That is, do not give them power over us so that they revile us and torture us. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said. Accordingly, *fitnah* (trial) is a *masdar* (verbal noun, used here to mean the one who is tried) in the sense of *maftun*, meaning "one who is tortured," from *fatana al-fiddah* (he melted the silver) when he melts it. It is as if it were said: "Our Lord, do not make us those who are tortured by those who disbelieve." Mujahid said: that is, do not torture us at their hands, or with a punishment from You, so that they think they are in the right and we are in the wrong, and thus they are tried by that.

Qatadah and Abu Mijlaz said something close to this, but the first view is more preferred. This supplicatory clause (*al-jumlah al-du'a'iyyah*) is not joined by conjunction to the clause before it, treating the two as separate items in a list (*al-jumal al-ma'dudah*), and the same applies to the clause that follows. It has been said that this clause is a *badal* (substitute or appositive) for what precedes it, but this was rejected because the two meanings are not identical, either as a whole or in part, and there is no connection between them other than that both are supplications.

﴿And forgive us﴾ our shortcomings ﴿our Lord, You are indeed the Almighty﴾, the Victorious who does not humiliate the one who takes refuge in Him, and does not disappoint the hope of the one who puts his trust in Him, ﴿the All-Wise﴾, who does nothing except that which contains profound wisdom.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 60, verse 6:

﴿There has indeed been for you in them﴾ i.e., in Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him, and those with him, ﴿an excellent example﴾. The discussion regarding it is similar to what preceded. And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾ i.e., His reward, the Exalted, or His meeting, glorified is He, and the bounties of the Hereafter, or the Days of Allah, the Exalted, and the Last Day specifically. The word "hope" (raja') may carry both expectation and fear. It is a complement (silah) to ﴿hasanah﴾ (excellent), or a qualifier (sifah). It has also been permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for "lakum" (for you), based on the view of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat) that it is permissible for a noun (zahir) to substitute for a pronoun of the second person, and likewise for a pronoun of the first person, as a substitute of the whole (badal al-kull), just as it is permissible to substitute it for a pronoun of the third person, and to substitute from the whole a substitute of part (badal al-ba'd), a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), and a substitute by error (badal al-ghalat).

It is also reported that the permissibility of that substitution is attributed to Sibawayh, but the majority hold it to be impermissible, and they restrict the permissibility to the substitute of part, the substitute of inclusion, and the substitute by error.
Page 74

Some of the eminent scholars mentioned that there is no disagreement about the permissibility of substituting, from the second-person pronoun, a substitute of the whole in what conveys encompassment, as in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿It shall be a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114]. He considered what is here to be of this kind, though there is some obscurity in that. As for the clause ﴿There has indeed been﴾ etc., it has been said that it is a repetition of what preceded, of the emphasis in exhorting emulation of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and those with him; and for this reason it is introduced with an oath. And it is, as al-Khafaji said: if His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿when they said﴾ is not taken into account, since it is a restrictive qualifier; but if it is taken into account, then this is generalization after specification. This is derived from the words of al-Tibi in establishing the matter of this repetition.

The apparent meaning is that this is restricted to something like what preceded, as if it were said: "There has indeed been for you in them an excellent example, when they said" etc. And in His, glorified is He, saying ﴿for whoever﴾ etc. there is an indication that whoever hopes for Allah, the Exalted, and the Last Day does not abandon following them, and that abandoning it is one of the signs of not hoping in Allah, glorified is He, and the Last Day, which is a characteristic of the disbelievers, rather one that indicates disbelief, as His, the Exalted's, saying indicates: ﴿And whoever turns away, then indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾, for it is of the kind of threat the disbelievers are warned with.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 60, verse 7:

﴿It may be that Allah will bring about affection between you and those among them whom you have taken as enemies.﴾ That is, from your polytheist relatives. ﴿Affection﴾ means that they would agree with you in religion. Allah the Exalted promised them this when He saw their firmness in religion and their strictness in opposing their fathers, their sons and all their other relatives, and their complete severance from them, so as to comfort their hearts. Allah, glorified is He, fulfilled His generous promise when He granted them the conquest, and their people embraced Islam, so the love and mutual purity that followed between them was complete. This includes Abu Sufyan and his like among the freed captives of the conquest of Mecca, from among their polytheist relatives.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Adi, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (the Proofs of Prophethood), and Ibn Asakir narrated through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: The affection that Allah the Exalted placed between them was the marriage of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Umm Habiba, daughter of Abu Sufyan, so she became the Mother of the Believers, and Mu'awiya became the maternal uncle of the believers. You know that her marriage took place at the time of the migration to Abyssinia (Habasha), while the revelation of these verses was in the sixth year after the hijra (migration). So what has been mentioned can hardly be sound on its apparent meaning, and there is discussion about its authenticity from Ibn Abbas.

﴿And Allah is All-Powerful﴾: intensifying in power, so He, glorified is He, is able to turn hearts, change conditions, and facilitate the causes of affection. ﴿And Allah is All-Forgiving﴾: intensifying in forgiveness, so He, majestic is His glory, forgives you for what has passed from you in your alliance with them. ﴿Most Merciful﴾: intensifying in mercy, so He, mighty and majestic, has mercy on you by uniting the scattered, by making treachery impossible, turning trust into confidence, and turning hatred into affection. It was also said: Allah, glorified is He, forgives those among the polytheists who embrace Islam and has mercy on them. The first view is more beneficial and more suitable to the context.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 60, verse 8:

﴿God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes, from being righteous to them﴾ That is: Glorified and Exalted is He, does not forbid you from showing kindness (al-birr) to these people, as is required by the fact that ﴿that you be righteous to them﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the relative pronoun. ﴿And deal justly with them﴾ That is: act toward them with justice (al-qist), i.e., equity (al-adl). So the verb is construed with the meaning of "reaching out to" (al-ifda'), which is why it takes ila (to). ﴿Indeed, God loves those who act justly﴾ That is, those who are equitable.

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "My mother came to me desiring (something), and she was a polytheist during the truce of Quraysh when they made a covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Should I maintain ties with her?' Then Allah revealed ﴿God does not forbid you﴾ etc., and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), upon him be prayers and peace, said: 'Yes, maintain ties with your mother.'" In the narration of Imam Ahmad and a group from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, he said: "Qutaylah bint Abd al-Uzza came to her daughter Asma' bint Abi Bakr with gifts of ṣināb (a kind of dried fruit/ pressed cheese-like item), aqit (dried curd), and butter, while she was a polytheist. Asma' refused to accept her gift or to let her into her house, until she sent to Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, asking her to inquire of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this. So she asked him, and Allah revealed ﴿God does not forbid you﴾, the verse, and he commanded her to accept her gift and let her into her house."

This Qutaylah, according to what is in al-Tahrir, was the wife of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, whom he divorced in the pre-Islamic period, and she is truly the mother of Asma'. Ibn Atiyyah narrated that she was her maternal aunt, and he called her "mother" figuratively. The first is the one relied upon. Al-Hasan and Abu Salih said: the verse was revealed concerning Khuza'ah, the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Kinanah, Muzaynah, and tribes of the Arabs who had made a treaty with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that they would not fight him nor aid against him. Qurrah al-Hamdani and Atiyyah al-Awfi said: it was revealed concerning a group of the Banu Hashim, among them al-Abbas.

From Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr: it was revealed concerning the women and children among the disbelievers. Mujahid said: concerning a people in Makkah who believed but did not migrate, so the Muhajirun and the Ansar were reluctant to show kindness to them because they had neglected the obligation of emigration. It was also said: concerning believers from Makkah and elsewhere who remained among the disbelievers and abandoned emigration, while being able to do so. Al-Nahhas and al-Tha'labi said: it was revealed concerning the oppressed believers who could not emigrate. Most scholars hold that it concerns disbelievers who possessed the characteristics mentioned in the relative clause. On this basis al-Kiya said: in it is evidence for the permissibility of giving charity to the dhimmis but not to the people of war (harbis), and for the obligation of maintaining a dhimmi father but not a harbi one, since his killing is obligatory. It occurs to me that I saw in the Fatawa al-Hadithiyyah of Ibn Hajar, may mercy be upon him, that he used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of standing up for the dhimmis, since it is a form of kindness and goodness toward them, and we have not been forbidden from it. However, when I reviewed those fatawa while writing this study I did not find that. Nevertheless, I found it quoted at the end of al-Fatawa al-Kubra, in the chapter on the sira, from al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam, that standing up for a disbeliever is not done, because we are commanded to humiliate him and display his lowliness. If great harm is feared from his evil, it is permitted, since uttering a word of disbelief is permitted under compulsion, so this is more fitting. He did not follow this with anything. Then, regarding whether standing is an act of kindness absolutely, there is hesitation, and al-Izz's restriction of the permissibility of standing for a disbeliever to cases where great harm is feared contradicts the statement of Ibn Wahban of the Hanafis:

"A disbeliever is served for inclination or for wealth, and for inclination toward Islam, if he stands, he is forgiven."

Some people make every religious benefit like inclination toward Islam, but on condition that the one standing does not intend veneration. And God knows best. Al-Khafaji, citing al-Durr al-Manthur, related that this verse is abrogated by the words of God Most High: ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], the verse. The use of it for what you have heard, assuming no abrogation, is valid only if it holds according to some of the views concerning it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 60, verse 9:

﴿God only forbids you from those who fight you over religion, expel you from your homes, and back others in your expulsion﴾ (like the polytheists of Mecca), for some of them strove to expel the believers and some of them aided the expellers. ﴿That you take them as allies﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the relative pronoun, also a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal). That is, He, glorified is He, only forbids you from taking them as allies. ﴿And whoever takes them as allies, those are the wrongdoers﴾, because they have placed loyalty in the place of enmity; or they are the wrongdoers against themselves by exposing themselves to punishment. In the restrictive form (hasr) there is an emphasis that is not hidden.

O you who have believed, this is a ruling for one who shows faith after the ruling on the two groups of disbelievers has been stated. ﴿When the believing women come to you﴾, meaning outwardly, ﴿as emigrants﴾ from among the disbelievers. It was also read as "muhajiratun" (emigrants, in the nominative) in apposition to ﴿the believing women﴾, as if it were said: when there come to you "emigrants." ﴿Then test them﴾, meaning examine them by what gives you a strong expectation that their hearts agree with their tongues in faith.

Abu al-Mundhir Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, Ibn Mardawayh, and a group related from Ibn 'Abbas, with a sound chain (isnad), that he said regarding how they were tested: When a woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ), 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, made her swear by Allah: "You did not leave out of desire for one land over another. By Allah, you did not leave out of hatred for a husband. By Allah, you did not leave seeking worldly gain. By Allah, you did not leave except out of love for Allah and His Messenger." In another report from him as well: The testing of the women was that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and he said: "Say to them: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, has taken your pledge that you will not associate anything with Allah," etc. ﴿Allah is most knowing﴾ of everyone, or of you, ﴿of their faith﴾, for He, glorified is He, is the one who has knowledge of what is in their hearts. The clause is a parenthetical insertion.

﴿Then if you know them﴾, meaning you think them to be so with a strong assumption that resembles knowledge after the testing, ﴿to be believers﴾ in reality, ﴿then do not return them to the disbelievers﴾, meaning to their disbelieving husbands, because of His saying: ﴿They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾. This is a reason (ta'lil) for the prohibition of returning them to them. The first clause explains the established separation and the certain ending of the first marriage. The second explains the impossibility of a marriage that is to be newly begun and established in the future. This is indicated by the use of a noun in the first and a verb in the second.

Al-Tayyibi said, regarding the reason for the difference between the two expressions: The attributive adjective (al-sifah al-mushabbahah) was attributed to the pronoun of the believing women in the first clause, to inform that this ruling, meaning the negation of lawfulness, is fixed in them, and that no breach or change is permissible on their part. The verb was attributed to the pronoun of the disbelievers, to signal that this ruling remains in force in future times, but it is capable of change by exchanging guidance for misguidance. It is also permissible that this is a repetition for emphasis and intensification in the prohibition and the cutting of the relationship. In this there is a kind of rhetorical device (badi') that some have named "reversal and exchange" (al-'aks wa al-tabdil), like that in His saying: ﴿They are garments for you and you are garments for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. Perhaps the first is more appropriate. The verse has been used as evidence that disbelievers are addressed concerning the subsidiary rulings (al-furu'), as in al-Intisaf. The view that the addressee regarding the believing woman is herself, and regarding the disbeliever are the rulers, in the sense that they are addressed to prevent that act from occurring, has an uncertain status. Talhah read: "la hunna yahlilna lahum" (they are not lawful for them).

﴿And give them what they have spent﴾, meaning give their husbands the like of what they paid them of bridal gifts. It was said: this is obligatory, and it was said: it is recommended. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ), in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, commanded 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, to write the treaty of peace. He wrote: "In Your name, O Allah. This is what Muhammad, son of 'Abd Allah, agreed upon with Suhayl ibn 'Amr. They agreed to suspend war among the people for ten years, during which the people will be safe and some will refrain from others, on the condition that whoever comes to Muhammad from Quraysh without the permission of his guardian, he will return him to them, and whoever comes to Quraysh from Muhammad, they will not return him to him. Between us is a closed chest (ʿaybah makfufah), and there is no secret theft (islal) and no treachery (ighlal). Whoever wishes to enter into the covenant and pact of Muhammad may enter it, and whoever wishes to enter into the covenant and pact of Quraysh may enter it." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl, and no man came to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, during the period of the covenant except that he returned him, even if he was a Muslim. Then the believing women came as emigrants. Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt was among those who went out to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and she was the first of the emigrant women. Her two brothers, 'Ammar and al-Walid, went out until they arrived before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they spoke with him about her matter, so that he would return her to Quraysh. Then the verse was revealed, and he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not return her to them. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) married her to Zayd ibn Haritha, may Allah be pleased with him.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muqatil that a woman called Suba'ah bint al-Harith al-Aslamiyah came as a believer. She had been married to Sayfi ibn al-Rahib, who was a polytheist from the people of Makkah. They asked for her return, so Allah revealed the verse. It is also narrated that she had been married to Musafir al-Makhzumi, and that he was given what he had spent, and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, married her. In another report, the verse was revealed concerning Umaymah bint Bishr, a woman from Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, who had been married to Abu Hassan ibn al-Dahdahah. She emigrated as a believer to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they asked for her return, so the verse was revealed, and he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not return her to them. Suhayl ibn Sayf married her, and she bore him 'Abd Allah ibn Suhayl. Perhaps the occasions of revelation are multiple. In any case, the verse, as has been said, was revealed as an explanation, because the condition in the treaty document applied only to men and not to women. The delay of the specifying (mukhassis) from the general ('amm) is permissible according to al-Jubba'i and those who agree with him. It is attributed to al-Zamakhshari that this is a delay of the explanation of the unspecified (mujmal), because he does not hold the generality of those expressions, but considers them unrestricted (mutlaq), and the reading as general or specific is according to the context. The Hanafis permit it. It cannot be said that this resembles a delay beyond the time of need, which is impermissible according to all, because the time of need, meaning acting upon the address, was after the arrival of the emigrant women and the demand for their return, not at the time the truce with Quraysh was made. Some Shafi'is also held this view. Among them is one who claimed that the generalisation came from the Prophet (ﷺ) by ijtihad (independent reasoning), for which he received one reward, and he was not confirmed in it. Among them is one who agreed with the majority of the Hanafis on abrogation (naskh), not specification (takhsis). Whoever permits abrogation of the Sunnah by the Qur'an says: it was abrogated by the verse. Whoever does not permit it says: it was abrogated by the Sunnah, namely the Prophet's (ﷺ) refraining from returning them, and the verse came confirming his action, peace and blessings be upon him.

It is narrated from al-Dahhak that there was a covenant between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the polytheists that no woman from among them would come to you who is not upon your religion except that you would return her to us. If she entered your religion while having a husband, then she would return to her husband who had spent on her. The Prophet (ﷺ) had a similar condition. Accordingly, the verse agrees with what the covenant stipulated. However, Abu Dawud in his al-Nasikh, Ibn Jarir, and others related from Qatadah that it abrogated this covenant and this ruling, meaning the giving to husbands of what they spent, in Bara'ah (al-Tawbah). As for the abrogation of the covenant, it is because of the command in it to renounce (al-nabdh). As for the abrogation of the ruling, it is because the ruling is a branch of the covenant, so when it is abrogated, it is abrogated. What the majority of Shafi'is hold is that the obligation of payment to their husbands is not established. This is explained in al-Kashf, on the view of the abrogation of the return of the woman, the view of specification, and the view that the generalisation was by ijtihad which he, peace and blessings be upon him, was not confirmed in. Then he said: As for the view of al-Dahhak, meaning the earlier one, it is problematic, its aspect being that it is a ruling about specific persons, so it does not generalise to other than that incident. Furthermore, He, mighty and majestic, restricted the ruling to the emigrants, and after the conquest there was no emigration, as is established in the Sahih, so the ruling does not remain.

﴿And there is no blame upon you to marry them﴾, meaning in marrying them, since their Islam has come between them and their disbelieving husbands, ﴿when you have given them their wages﴾, meaning at the time of your giving them their bridal payments. ﴿Then﴾ is merely for the sense of time, and it is permissible for it to be conditional, with its answer omitted, by the evidence of what came before. Under both readings, the requirement of giving bridal payments is understood as a condition for the removal of blame from marrying them. The intended meaning of giving the wages is not handing them over physically but undertaking and committing to them. The apparent meaning of this, together with what preceded in His saying ﴿and give them what they have spent﴾, is that there is a giving to the husbands and a giving to the women. So what was given to the husbands does not replace their bridal payments, but their bridal payments must also be given. It was said: it is either that by the wages is meant what was paid to them so that they would pay it to their husbands, and so the permission to marry them is conditioned upon the prior payment of it, or that if it was given to them as a loan, and they then married upon that, there is no harm. Or it is made clear to them that what was given to their husbands does not replace the bridal payment. This is what we mentioned first as the apparent meaning and the more correct ruling, while the other two views are weak in jurisprudence and in wording.

Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, used the verse as evidence that if one of the spouses leaves the abode of war as a Muslim or under protection (dhimmah), while the other remains a combatant (harbi), separation occurs. He does not hold that the emigrant woman must observe a waiting period ('iddah), and he permits marrying her without a waiting period unless she is pregnant. This is on the basis of the well-known hadith, by which an addition to the text is permitted: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him not water another's crop with his water." The position of al-Shafi'i, as it is said, is that separation occurs only with her Islam, and not merely by leaving. If she becomes Muslim before consummation, the separation takes effect immediately, and after consummation it is suspended until the end of the waiting period. The argument has been criticised on the grounds that the verse does not indicate all that was mentioned. Indeed, it has been used as evidence for the absence of a waiting period in separation by a woman's coming out to us from the abode of war as a Muslim. It was argued that He, glorified is He, negated blame in every respect in marrying the emigrant women after giving the bridal payment, and did not restrict it by the lapse of a waiting period. So if separation occurred merely by reaching the abode of Islam, there would be blame in a second marriage. Nevertheless, it has been said: the reply according to the principle of the Shafi'is is that lifting an unrestricted ruling is not an explicit abrogation, because not addressing something is not an address to its non-existence. As for the principle of the Hanafis, it is like other impediments. Her being pregnant is by consensus, so reflect.

﴿And do not hold on to marriage bonds with disbelieving women﴾. ʿIṣam (bonds) is the plural of ʿiṣmah, which is what one holds to for protection, from a contract or a cause. The intended meaning is the prohibition for the believers against having between themselves and the polytheist wives who remain in the abode of war any bond of marriage at all, so that one of them would not prevent a fifth marriage or a marriage to her sister during the waiting period, on the basis that they have no waiting period. Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever has a disbelieving wife in Makkah, let him not count her among his wives, because the difference of the two abodes has cut off her bond with him. Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he said: the saying of Him, exalted is He, ﴿And do not hold on﴾ and so on, was revealed concerning a Muslim woman who joined the polytheists, so her husband did not hold on to her bond, for he had disowned her.

Also related: Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar to it. In another narration from Mujahid, he said: Allah, glorified is He, commanded them to divorce the wives who remained with the disbelievers and to separate from them. It is also related that ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, divorced for this reason his wife Fatimah, sister of Umm Salamah, daughter of Abu Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi, and Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan married her. And his wife Kulthum bint Jarwal al-Khuza'i was married by Abu Jahm ibn Hudhayfah al-ʿAdawi. Likewise, Talhah divorced his wife Arwa bint Rabi'ah. This has been objected to on the grounds that, taken at face value, it contradicts the position of the Hanafis and the Shafi'is. As for the Hanafis, separation occurs by the very fact of arrival in the abode of Islam. As for the Shafi'is, the divorce is suspended: if the two are brought together within the waiting period (ʿiddah), it is shown that it took effect from the moment of the utterance; otherwise, the separation is final by virtue of the woman's remaining in disbelief. Thus the apparent meaning of the verse does not indicate what is in this narration.

Abu ʿAmr, Mujahid (in one of the reported readings from him), Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and al-A'raj read ﴿تَمَسَّكُوا﴾ as the imperfect of the form مَسَكَ with a doubled sin (تَمَسَّكُوا, "tamassakū", from مَسَّكَ, intensive form). Al-Hasan also, together with Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn ʿAmir (in the narration of ʿAbd al-Hamid), and Abu ʿAmr (in the narration of Muʿadh), read ﴿تَمَسَّكُوا﴾ as the imperfect of تَمَسَّكَ with one of the two tā' elided; the original is تَتَمَسَّكُوا.

Al-Hasan also read ﴿تَمْسِكُوا﴾ with a kasrah on the sin, as the imperfect of the triliteral مَسَكَ.

﴿وَاسْأَلُوا مَا أَنْفَقْتُمْ﴾: that is, ask the disbelievers for the dowries (muhur) of your wives who have gone over to them. ﴿وَلْيَسْأَلُوا مَا أَنْفَقُوا﴾: that is, let the disbelievers ask you for the dowries of their wives who emigrated to you. Its apparent form is a command to the disbelievers, but it is of the same type as ﴿وَلْيَجِدُوا فِيكُمْ غِلْظَةً﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123]; so it is a command to the believers to pay, used figuratively.

It has been said that what is meant is equity (al-taswiyah). ﴿ذَلِكُمْ﴾, that which has been mentioned, ﴿حُكْمُ اللَّهِ﴾ is the judgment of Allah; so follow it. His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿يَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكُمْ﴾ is either a new, independent statement, or a circumstantial clause (hal) related to ﴿حُكْمُ﴾ with the returning pronoun omitted, in which case it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq): that is, Allah judges it among you. Or the returning pronoun is the hidden pronoun within ﴿يَحْكُمُ﴾, by making the judgment itself a judge, as an intensification, as if the judgment, because of its strength and clarity, does not need another judge. ﴿وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمٌ﴾: He legislates what wisdom that is perfect requires.

It is related that when this ruling was established, the believers paid from what they had been commanded regarding the dowries of the emigrant women to their husbands, while the polytheists refused to pay any of the dowries of the disbelieving women to their believing husbands. Then it was revealed.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿And if there escapes from you﴾, i.e., outstrips you and gets away from you, ﴿anything of your wives to the disbelievers﴾, i.e., any one of your wives. This is also how it has been recited. The use of *shay'* (thing) in this position is for added generality and to include the most insignificant category, explicitly. In al-Kashshaf (the Kashshaf of al-Zamakhshari), you may say: the intention is belittlement and disparagement directed at the Muslims, because whoever of their wives escapes to the disbelievers deserves humiliation and disgrace. The escaped wives were six in number, as al-Zamakhshari reports and details them in the Kashshaf. Alternatively, ﴿anything fled from you﴾ refers to the *mahr* (bridal gift) of your wives, with *shay'* used in its literal sense for non-rational things, and *min* (from) being *ibtida'iyyah* (indicating origin) rather than *bayaniyyah* (explanatory), as in the first interpretation. ﴿Then you gained⁠﴾ is from *al-'uqbah* (turn), not from *al-'iqab* (punishment). Originally it means the turn in riding one of two companions' mount, with the other riding after him; i.e., ﴿then your turn came⁠﴾, meaning your turn to pay the *mahr*. This likens the ruling applied to the Muslims and the disbelievers, namely that these people pay the *mahr* of those people's wives at one time, and those people pay the *mahr* of these people's wives at another. Or it likens the ruling of the aforementioned payment to a matter in which they take turns, just as turns are taken in riding. The summary of the meaning is: if one of your wives joins the disbelievers, or some of their *mahr* escapes you, and you are obligated to pay the *mahr*, just as the disbelievers were obligated.

﴿So give to those whose wives have gone the equivalent of what they spent⁠﴾ from the *mahr* of the emigrant women whom you married, and do not give it to her disbelieving husband, so that it may be a retribution (*qisas*). From what we have mentioned, it is known that *'aqaba* does not imply reciprocity. This is like when you say: "camels that are *mu'aqaba*, grazing on saltwort plants at one time and other things at another," and you do not mean that they take turns with other camels in that. Understanding the verse in this sense agrees with what is reported from al-Zuhri, who said: "Whoever's wife has joined the disbelievers is given from the dowry of whoever's wives have joined the Muslims."

From al-Zajjaj it is reported that the meaning of ﴿fa-'aqabtum⁠﴾ is *fa-ghanimtum* (then you gained spoils), and its reality is *fa-asabtum fi al-qital bi-'uqubah* (then you obtained, in fighting, a turn of success) until you gained spoils. It is as if it were said: ﴿And if there escapes from you anything of your wives to the disbelievers⁠﴾ and they do not pay you their *mahr*, then you gain from them ﴿so give to those whose wives have gone the equivalent of what they spent⁠﴾ from the *ghanimah* (spoils). This is the interpretation, rather than what preceded. The Prophet (ﷺ), as reported from Ibn 'Abbas, used to give the one whose wife had gone the *mahr* from the spoils before they were divided into fifths, and he did not diminish his right in any way. Ibn Jinni said: We have been told from Qutrub that he said: ﴿fa-'aqabtum⁠﴾ means *fa-asabtum 'aqaban minhum* (then you obtained a turn from them), as one says: "'aqaba al-rajulu shay'an" (the man took a thing) when he took something. In meaning it is like the interpretation before it.

Mujahid, al-Zuhri, al-A'raj, Ikrimah, Humayd, Abu Haywah, and al-Za'farani recited ﴿fa-'aqqabtum⁠﴾ with a doubled *qaf*, from *'aqabahu* when he followed him, because each of the two alternating parties follows the other. Al-Zuhri, al-A'raj, Abu Haywah also, and al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab (with a variant from him) recited ﴿fa-'aqabtum⁠﴾ with a *fatha* on the *qaf* and without doubling. Al-Zuhri and al-Nakha'i also recited it with a *kasra* and without doubling. Mujahid also recited ﴿fa-a'qabtum⁠﴾, meaning you entered into the *'aqabah* (turn). Al-Zajjaj interpreted these four readings as meaning: ﴿then the outcome was yours⁠﴾, i.e., victory and triumph, until you gained spoils, because that is the outcome that deserves to be called an outcome.

﴿And fear God, in whom you believe⁠﴾, for belief in Him, Mighty and Majestic, requires fear of Him, glorified be He.

**Page 80**

Meaning: they are those who pledge allegiance to you, that is, those who intend to pledge allegiance. ﴿On condition that they do not associate anything with God﴾, that is, anything among things, or any kind of association (*shirk*). ﴿Nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill their children﴾. As many have said, this refers to the burying of daughters alive, as indicated by external evidence, although "children" is more general than "daughters." It is also permitted to keep the phrase on its apparent meaning, since the Arabs used to do this out of poverty and destitution. Consider whether it is permissible to extend this prohibition to cover that as well, and also to the abortion of a fetus after the soul has been breathed into it. ʿAlī, may God honor his face, al-Ḥasan and al-Sulamī read *"wa-lā yuqattilna"* with the doubled letter (shaddah). ﴿Nor bring a slander which they have invented between their hands and their feet﴾.

Al-Farrāʾ said: In the pre-Islamic era, a woman would pick up a newborn and say, "This is my child from you," and that is the invented slander "between their hands and their feet," because when the mother gives birth, the child falls between her hands and feet. In *al-Kashshāf* it is stated that the invented slander "between her hands and her feet" is a metaphor for the child whom she attributes falsely to her husband, because the belly in which she carries it is "between the hands," and her womb through which she gives birth is "between the feet." It was also said that this is a metaphor for an adopted child (*daʿī*), because the women who would show their bellies to their husbands at the beginning of the matter did so only to make a favor of it to them, and at the second stage, at the time of labor, when they would deliver the child between their legs, they would claim that they had borne it for them. Thus they were forbidden from that which is a sign of the pre-Islamic era and contrary to the sign of Muslim women, depicting those two states and denouncing what they used to do. In any case, interpreting the verse as described above is the view of most scholars, and it is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both. Some eminent scholars said: its meaning is, "They shall not bring a slander from their own selves," and the hand and foot are a metaphor for the self, because most actions are done by them. For this reason it is said of one punished for a verbal offense, "This is what your hands have earned." Or its meaning is, "They shall not bring a slander which they fabricate in their own hearts and minds," and the heart is situated between the hands and feet. The statement under the first interpretation is a metaphor for fabricating slander from their own selves; under the second, it is a metaphor for slander arising from the inner corruption of their hearts.

Al-Khaṭṭābī said: its meaning is, "They shall not slander people face to face and openly," just as it is said of a matter in your presence, "It is between your hands." This was refuted by saying that although they use the above expression for someone present, one does not say of it, "It is between your feet." This would be valid if the feet were mentioned alone, but when they are mentioned together with the hands as a follower, it is not valid. It has been said that the expression is a metaphor for tearing the veil of modesty, and the intended meaning is a prohibition of slander, which includes lying and backbiting. It is related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that he interpreted it as referring to slander (*qadhf*). It was also said: "between their hands" means a kiss or touching, and "their feet" means intercourse. It was also said: "between their hands" means their tongues with gossip, and "their feet" means their private parts with intercourse. This, and what precedes it, are as you see.

It was also said: "slander" means magic, and women have a strong inclination toward it, so they were forbidden from it. But this is not correct.

﴿Nor disobey you in what is right﴾, that is, in what you command them of what is good and forbid them from what is wrong. The restriction to "what is right," although the Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, commands only what is right, serves to alert that obedience to a created being is not permissible in disobedience to the Creator. This refutes those ignorant people who claim that obedience to those in authority is obligatory without any condition. Some scholars restricted this "right" to the abandonment of wailing for the dead, based on what Imām Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī (who graded it *ḥasan*), Ibn Mājah and others related: "From Umm Salamah al-Anṣāriyyah, who said: A woman from among these women said, 'What is this right thing that it is not fitting for us to disobey you in?' He, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Do not wail.'" The hadith continues. Many similar reports apparently restrict it to what has been mentioned. But the correct view is generality, and what is mentioned in the reports is by way of limiting the general to some of its instances for a specific reason. Generality is supported by the statement of Ibn ʿAbbās, Anas and Zayd ibn Aslam: "It is wailing, tearing the collars, tattooing the faces, joining hair, and other things of the Sacred Law that He made obligatory or recommended." The specific mention of the matters enumerated with regard to women is due to their frequent occurrence among them, along with the fact that some of them are specific to women, as you have heard earlier.

**Page 81**

﴿So accept their pledge﴾, by guaranteeing reward for fulfilling these matters. The restriction of their pledge to what was mentioned, namely their coming, is to urge them to hasten toward it with complete desire, without any invitation from him to them. ﴿And ask God's forgiveness for them﴾, in addition to the guarantee of reward implicit in the pledge. ﴿Indeed God is All-Forgiving, All-Merciful﴾, that is, He, exalted is His majesty, is exceedingly forgiving and merciful, so He will forgive them and show mercy to them, mighty and majestic is He, if they fulfill what they pledged to.

This verse was revealed, as Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Muqātil, on the day of the Conquest (of Mecca). The Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, pledged allegiance to the men at al-Ṣafā, while ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, pledged allegiance to the women beneath it, on behalf of the Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him. It is also reported that the Messenger, peace be upon him, pledged allegiance to the women personally as well.

Al-Imām Aḥmad, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, al-Tirmidhī (who graded it *ṣaḥīḥ*) and others related from Umaymah bint Ruqayqah, who said: "I came to the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, to pledge allegiance to him, and he took from us what is in the Qur'an: that we would not associate anything with God, until he reached 'nor disobey you in what is right.' He said: 'In what you are able to and can bear.' We said: 'God and His Messenger are more merciful to us than we are to ourselves, O Messenger of God. Will you not shake hands with us?' He said: 'I do not shake hands with women. My word to a hundred women is like my word to one woman.'"

Sa'īd ibn Manṣūr and Ibn Saʿd related from al-Shaʿbī, who said: "When the Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, pledged allegiance to women, he placed a cloth over his hand." In some reports it is that he, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, would pledge allegiance to them while between his hands and their hands there was a folded cloth. Whoever affirms this says there was handshaking at the time of the pledge, but the most well-known and relied-upon view is that there was no handshaking. Ibn Saʿd and Ibn Mardawayh related from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "When the Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, pledged allegiance to women, he would call for a vessel of water, dip his hand into it, and then the women would dip their hands into it. It seems this was a substitute for handshaking." And God knows best its authenticity.

The pledge of allegiance took place on more than one occasion. It occurred in Mecca after the Conquest and in Medina. Among those who pledged allegiance to him, peace be upon him, in Mecca was Hind bint ʿUtbah, the wife of Abū Sufyān. In the hadith of Asmāʾ bint Yazīd ibn al-Sakan: "I was among the women who pledged allegiance, and Hind bint ʿUtbah was among the women. The Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, recited the verse to them. When he reached, 'On condition that they do not associate anything with God,' Hind said: 'How can we hope that He will accept from us what He has not accepted from the men?' She meant that the obligation of this was clear. When he reached, 'Nor steal,' she said: 'By God, I take a little from the property of Abū Sufyān, and I do not know whether it is lawful for me.' Abū Sufyān said: 'Whatever you have taken in the past and in the future is lawful for you.' The Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, laughed, recognized her, and said to her: 'Are you indeed Hind bint ʿUtbah?' She said: 'Yes. So pardon what has passed, O Prophet of God. May God pardon you.' He said: 'Nor commit adultery.' She said: 'Does a free woman commit adultery?' She meant that adultery occurs among slave women, based on what was the custom in the pre-Islamic era, that a free woman generally does not commit adultery, and that it is mostly slave women who do. The qualification 'generally' was added because it was said that the women with banners were free women. He said: 'Nor kill their children.' She said: 'We raised them as infants, and you killed them as adults,' meaning what happened with her son Ḥanẓalah ibn Abī Sufyān, who was killed on the day of Badr. ʿUmar laughed until he lay on his back, and the Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, smiled. In another version, she said: 'You killed the fathers, and you ask us to care for the children?!' The Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, laughed. He said: 'Nor bring a slander.' She said: 'By God, slander is indeed a shameful matter, and God does not command except what is right and noble conduct.' He said: 'Nor disobey you in what is right.' She said: 'By God, we did not sit in this gathering of ours with the intention of disobeying you in anything.'" It seems this was said by her rather than by other women because of the standing of Umm Ḥabībah, may God be pleased with her, with the Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, even though she was recently converted from the pre-Islamic era.

It is related that the first women to pledge allegiance to the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, were the mother of Saʿd ibn Muʿādh and Kabshah bint Rāfiʿ, along with other women, may God be pleased with them all.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 60, verse 13:**

﴿O you who have believed, do not take as allies a people with whom God is angry﴾. It is narrated from al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Mundhir ibn Sa'id that they are the Jews, because He, Exalted and Majestic, has described them elsewhere, in other than this verse, as "those who have earned His anger" (al-maghdub 'alayhim). It is also reported that some of the poorer believers used to associate with the Jews in order to obtain some of their fruits, and so this verse was revealed. It has been said: they are the Jews and the Christians. In a report from Ibn 'Abbas, they are the disbelievers of Quraysh. Others have said: they are the disbelievers in general. This verse, according to al-Tibi, is connected to the conclusion of the account of the polytheists, whom the believers were forbidden to take as allies, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], and it is His saying: ﴿Whoever takes them as allies, those are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 9]. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, when believing women come to you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], and so on, is a digression (istitrad). For when the discussion of dealing with those who do not fight the Muslims, and with those who fight them and have driven them out of their homes, had reached the command to show kindness to the former and the prohibition of showing kindness to the latter, He introduced the matter of dealing with their women. When He had finished with that, He connected the conclusion to the opening, in the manner of radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr (returning the end to the beginning) in terms of meaning. In al-Intisaf, the author made this verse itself a digression. This is evident according to the view that the people meant are the Jews, or the People of the Book in general.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They have despaired of the Hereafter﴾ is a resumed sentence (isti'naf). What is meant is that they have despaired of the good of the Hereafter and its reward, because of their obstinacy towards the Messenger (ﷺ), whose description is in their Scripture, who was supported by clear signs and dazzling miracles. If the people meant are the disbelievers, then their despair of the Hereafter is because of their disbelief in it.

﴿As the disbelievers have despaired of those in the graves﴾: that is, those who are the people of the graves, namely the dead disbelievers, with "min" (مِن) being explanatory (bayaniyyah). The meaning is that the despair of these people regarding the Hereafter is like the despair of the disbelievers who died, entered the graves, and became certain of their deprivation of its lasting bliss. It has also been said: it is like their despair of ever attaining any good from these living people. The purpose is to describe them with complete despair regarding the Hereafter. That "min" is explanatory is related from Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd, and it is the preference of Ibn 'Atiyyah and a group. Abu Hayyan preferred that it be for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah). The meaning then is that these people, the wrathful-against people, have despaired of the Hereafter just as they have despaired of their dead being raised and meeting them in the life of this world. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah. In this case, "the disbelievers" means those people, and the apparent noun has been placed in the position of their pronoun, to record their disbelief and to indicate the reason for their despair. Ibn Abi al-Zinad read kama ya'isa al-kafir (كَما يَئِسَ الكافِرُ), in the singular, intending the genus.

* * *

Furthermore, among the allusive interpretations (min bab al-isharah fi ba'd al-ayat) is what has been said: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾, and so on, is an allusion for the wayfarer (al-salik) to abandon allying himself with the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammarah) and casting affection towards it, for it is the greatest enemy, as has been said: "The enemy most hostile to you is your self that lies between your two sides." It never ceases to hate the truth, to oppose the Messenger of reason, and to flee from him, and it does not cease from that until it becomes the tranquil self (al-nafs al-mutma'innah), content and pleasing. To this the allusion is in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps God will place affection between you and those among them with whom you have been at enmity﴾. And His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿God does not forbid you﴾, and so on, is an allusion to the fact that when the self obeys and its unruliness is secured, it is permissible to give it its permitted portions. To this the allusion is in what is reported: "Your self has a right over you" (li-nafsika 'alayka haqqan). And in His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you﴾, and so on, is an allusion to the pledge of allegiance of the guiding master to the sincere seeker whose self has become believing. This is that he pledges to him: to abandon choice and entrust affairs to God, Mighty and Majestic; not to desire what is not fitting for him; not to plunge into the desires of the self; not to bury the inspired inflow (al-warid al-ilhami) beneath the dust of nature; not to fabricate, claiming that a secret thought is the thought of the spirit and the thought of the spirit is the thought of the Truth, and so on; not to disobey in what is good that gives him the knowledge of God, Mighty and Majestic; and that he seek from God, Glorified is He, within the sphere of exaggeration (fi dimn al-mubalaghah), that He conceal his attributes with His attributes and his existence with His existence. Its sum is that subsistence be sought for him after annihilation (al-fana'), and that is the bounty of God which He gives to whom He wills.
